taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Kew also accepts Juniperus virginiana var. virginiana; the Central Texas/Williamson treatment uses var. virginiana. The learner remains at species rank for consistency.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Juniperus virginiana as native to Texas.
Travis County — the Travis County flora treats J. virginiana as a native tree, common in the eastern half of the county, with numerous TEX-LL sheets.
Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed local treatment of J. virginiana var. virginiana.

Bexar County — a U.S. EPA ecological risk assessment for Live Oak, Bexar County describes an adjacent wooded area of native trees and grasses and explicitly lists eastern red cedar (J. virginiana) among the larger trees.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Eastern redcedar is widely planted. County proof uses county flora/local ecological documentation, not ornamental plantings or the user's observations.

morphology.look_here_first: If a female tree has cones, start there: eastern redcedar has small glaucous blue-black cones about 4.5–5 mm across, commonly with 1–2(–3) seeds. Then inspect an adult scale leaf: the resin gland is pit-like/depressed near the base rather than a raised rounded mid-blade gland. Ashe juniper usually has larger 6.5–9.6 mm cones with one seed and a raised circular-to-hemispheric gland.
diagnostic_traits: evergreen dioecious small to medium tree, often with a single trunk and conic/columnar crown when young
adult foliage shoots slender, approximately four-sided, with closely appressed opposite scale leaves
adult scale leaves about 1 mm long, dark green and often slightly glossy
resin gland expressed as a small pit/depression near the basal-central part of the scale leaf
vigorous juvenile/whip shoots may carry longer sharp awl-shaped leaves
bark red-brown, thin and exfoliating/shredding in strips
mature berrylike seed cones small, about 4.5–5 mm, glaucous blue-black
seed cones commonly 1–2(–3)-seeded, often with one seed larger
more associated with Blackland Prairie/Post Oak/eastern or mesic sites than the dry limestone cedar-break dominance of Ashe juniper

confusers.separator: Best split: J. virginiana has a pit-like scale-leaf gland and smaller 4.5–5 mm cones commonly with 1–2(–3) seeds; J. ashei has a raised rounded/hemispheric gland and larger 6.5–9.6 mm cones usually with one seed. Habit/ecology support the ID: redcedar is often single-trunked/conic and more eastern/mesic, while Ashe juniper dominates dry Edwards Plateau limestone.

Kew currently treats var. ovata within J. ashei. It can be multi-seeded and complicates seed-count-only IDs, so confirm leaf-gland form and the full cone/foliage package rather than using seed number alone.
Redberry juniper has coppery to reddish-brown mature cones rather than the dark glaucous blue-black cones of eastern redcedar and Ashe juniper.

diagnostic_roles: adult scale-leaf gland macro showing pit/depression
small blue-black female cone with scale
direct J. ashei cone-size and leaf-gland comparison
eastern/mesic or Blackland/Post Oak habitat context
photo_verification.provenance_note: The most valuable learner photos are a macro of the scale-leaf gland and a measured mature cone opened to show seed number; generic tree-shape photos are secondary.
